title: Pneumatics: air supply, cylinders, 5/2 and 5/3 valves, ISO 1219 symbols
goals: Trace compressed air from the compressor to a cylinder, and say what each part of the supply does
Work out a cylinder's push and pull force from its bore, rod and pressure
Read a valve's name (3/2, 5/2, 5/3) and its ISO 1219 symbol, including the port numbers
Say what a 5/3 valve's centre does, and what a single- or double-solenoid valve does when power is lost
Make pneumatic kit safe before working on it
summary:
**Compressed air** is made by a **compressor**, stored in a **receiver**, dried by a **dryer**, then cleaned and set at each machine by an **FRL**: **f**ilter, **r**egulator (sets the pressure, typically about 6 bar), sometimes a **l**ubricator.

**Cylinders** turn air pressure into a straight push. **Single-acting**: air one way, a spring back. **Double-acting**: air both ways.

Force $F = pA$. With p in bar and A in mm², $F = 0.1 \times p \times A$ newtons (1 bar = 0.1 N/mm²). Push uses the full bore area $\frac{\pi D^2}{4}$; pull uses the **annulus**, the bore less the rod: $\frac{\pi (D^2 - d^2)}{4}$, so it is weaker.

**Valves** are named **ports/positions**. A **3/2** drives a single-acting cylinder; a **5/2** a double-acting one; a **5/3** has a middle position too:

- **closed centre**: all ports blocked, the cylinder is held (only roughly: air compresses and leaks)
- **exhaust (open) centre**: both cylinder ports vent: the piston is free
- **pressure centre**: both ports fed

**ISO 1219** symbols draw each position as a square, with arrows for the flow paths and ⊥ for blocked ports. Ports (ISO 5599): **1** supply, **2** and **4** outlets, **3** and **5** exhausts; pilot **14** connects 1 to 4, pilot **12** connects 1 to 2.

**Single solenoid with spring return** (monostable): on power loss it springs back. **Double solenoid** (bistable): it stays where it was, a memory.

Control speed with **flow controls on the exhaust** (meter-out) for a steady stroke.

**Safety**: air is stored energy. Isolate and **dump** the air (a lockable dump valve), and remember closed-centre valves and check valves can trap air in a cylinder.
sources: ISO 1219-1: Fluid power systems and components. Graphical symbols and circuit diagrams. Part 1: Graphical symbols
ISO 5599-3: Pneumatic fluid power. Five-port directional control valves. Part 3: Code system for communication of valve functions (port numbering)
ISO 4414: Pneumatic fluid power. General rules and safety requirements for systems and their components
Parr, A.: Hydraulics and Pneumatics: A Technician's and Engineer's Guide, 3rd edition (Butterworth-Heinemann)

formulas.name: Cylinder force
formulas.says: The pressure pushing on every square millimetre of the piston, times how many square millimetres there are.
symbols: the area the air pushes on (mm²)

formulas.name: Annulus area (the pull side)
formulas.says: On the rod side, the rod takes up part of the piston face, so the air pushes on a ring: the bore's area less the rod's.

bench.task: On a pneumatic machine you are authorised to work on, find the supply and the valves, with the machine isolated and the air dumped.
check: Find the FRL and read the regulator's pressure gauge before isolating
Close and lock the isolating (dump) valve and check the gauge falls to 0
Find a valve and read its symbol on the label: ports, positions, how it is operated
Look for anything that can still hold air (closed-centre valves, check valves, an air receiver on the machine)

cards.q: A solenoid valve on a machine is labelled 5/2. What does that mean?
options: 5 ports and 2 positions
5 bar and 2 litres a second
5 mm bore and 2 solenoids
Model 5, version 2
cards.why: Valves are named ports/positions. A 5/2 has a supply, two outlets and two exhausts, and two positions: the usual valve for a double-acting cylinder.

cards.title: From the compressor to the machine
cards.body:
- **Compressor**: squeezes air, usually to 7–10 bar.
- **Receiver**: a tank that stores it and evens out demand.
- **Dryer**: takes out the water that compressing makes.
- Pipework round the site, with drains at low points.
- At each machine an **FRL**: **filter** (dirt and water), **regulator** (sets the working pressure, often about 6 bar, with a gauge), sometimes a **lubricator**.
- A lockable **isolating/dump valve**, then the **valves** and **cylinders**.
cards.more:
Squeezing air heats it and concentrates its moisture; as it cools in the pipes, water drops out. Water in valves and cylinders washes out grease and causes rust and sticking, which is why dryers, drains and filters matter.

The regulator sets the pressure the machine actually uses. Set it lower than the main and the machine is not upset by the main's pressure swinging as other machines draw air.

Lubricators are less common now: most modern valves and cylinders are greased for life and oil in the air can wash that grease out.

cards.q: Put the air's path in order.
cards.why: Make it, store it, dry it, clean and set it at the machine, then switch it to the actuator.

cards.title: Cylinder force: F = pA
cards.body:
The air pushes on every square millimetre of the piston. **Force** = pressure × area:

$$F = pA$$

Use pressure in N/mm²: **1 bar = 0.1 N/mm²**, so 6 bar is 0.6 N/mm². The area of the **bore** (diameter $D$): $\frac{\pi D^2}{4}$.

On the way **back** (pull), the rod takes up part of the piston, so the air pushes on a ring, the **annulus**: $\frac{\pi (D^2 - d^2)}{4}$, with $d$ the rod. The pull is always weaker than the push.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 50 mm bore. Area: $\pi \times 50^2 \div 4 = 1963$ mm². At 6 bar (0.6 N/mm²): $0.6 \times 1963 = 1178$ N, about 120 kg of push.

With a 20 mm rod, the pull side's area is $\pi \times (2500 - 400) \div 4 = 1649$ mm², so the pull is $0.6 \times 1649 = 989$ N.

In practice friction and the need to accelerate take a share: size a cylinder so the load needs no more than about 70% of the theoretical force (less for fast moves).

cards.q: A cylinder with a {bore} mm bore runs at {bar} bar. What force does it push with, ignoring friction?
cards.why: Area of the bore, times the pressure in N/mm² (bar × 0.1). Using bar straight, without the 0.1, gives ten times the force.
cards.hint: Area from the bore, then × the pressure in N/mm² (1 bar = 0.1 N/mm²).

cards.title: Valves: ports and positions
cards.body:
A directional valve is named **ports/positions**:

- **3/2**: supply, one outlet, one exhaust; two positions. Drives a **single-acting** cylinder (spring return).
- **5/2**: supply, two outlets, two exhausts; two positions. Drives a **double-acting** cylinder: one outlet to each end.
- **5/3**: as 5/2, plus a **middle position**.

Operated by a **solenoid**, an air **pilot**, a lever or button, and returned by a **spring** or a second solenoid.
cards.more:
Count the holes and the states. A 5/2 has five holes: one in from the supply, two out to the cylinder's two ends, two out to exhaust. In one position, supply goes to one end and the other end vents; switch over and they swap. That drives a double-acting cylinder out and back.

A 3/2 only has one outlet: in one position it feeds the cylinder, in the other it vents it, and a spring in the cylinder brings it back.

Most solenoid valves are actually **pilot operated**: the solenoid moves a tiny valve whose air moves the main spool, so a small coil can switch a big valve.

cards.q: Which valve drives a double-acting cylinder out and back?
options: A 5/2 valve
A 3/2 valve
A 2/2 valve
A non-return valve
cards.why: A double-acting cylinder needs air to one end while the other end vents, then the other way round: a 5/2 (or 4/2) does that. A 3/2 feeds and vents one end only.

cards.title: Reading an ISO 1219 valve symbol
cards.body:
In an **ISO 1219** symbol:

- each **square** is one position; the number of squares is the number of positions
- **arrows** inside show where air flows in that position; a **⊥** is a blocked port
- the ports are drawn on the position the valve sits in at rest
- the operators are drawn at the ends: a box with a slash for a **solenoid**, a zigzag for a **spring**

Ports are numbered (ISO 5599): **1** supply, **2** and **4** outlets, **3** and **5** exhausts. A pilot signal **14** connects 1 to 4; **12** connects 1 to 2.
cards.more:
Read it like a slide that can move left or right. The pipes stay where they are; the squares slide under them. Whichever square sits under the pipes is the valve's state.

A single-solenoid 5/2 has the spring on one side and the solenoid on the other. At rest the spring pushes its square under the pipes: typically 1 to 2, and 4 to exhaust 5. Energise the coil and the other square slides in: 1 to 4, 2 to exhaust 3.

The numbers help on a real valve too: the supply hose goes to 1, the cylinder to 2 and 4, silencers on 3 and 5.

cards.q: Match each port number on a 5/2 valve with its job.
cards.why: ISO 5599 numbering: odd for supply and exhausts, even for outlets; a pilot's number says which ports it joins.

cards.title: 5/3 valves and their centre
cards.body:
A **5/3** valve has a middle position, held by springs when neither solenoid is on. What it does there depends on its **centre**:

- **Closed centre**: every port blocked. The cylinder stops and is held, only roughly (air compresses, and seals leak).
- **Exhaust (open) centre**: both cylinder ports vent. The piston is free to be pushed by hand, and nothing is held.
- **Pressure centre**: both ports fed. The piston creeps towards the rod end, because the full bore side has more area.
cards.more:
Picture three rooms for the slide to stop in. A 5/2 only has two, so its cylinder is always going one way or the other. A 5/3's middle room gives a 'stop' state.

Closed centre is used to stop mid-stroke. But air is springy: a load on the rod squashes or stretches the trapped air, so the rod gives a little, and a leak lets it drift. For a true hold, use a rod lock or brake.

Exhaust centre is used where, with power off, someone must be able to move the mechanism freely, or where a stop must also mean no force.

Whichever centre, the springs centre the valve on power loss, so the centre is also the valve's power-off state.

cards.q: Match each 5/3 centre with what the cylinder does in it.
pairs: Stops and is held roughly where it is
Both sides vent: the piston is free
Both sides fed: it creeps towards extending
cards.why: The centre is what the valve does with neither solenoid on, which includes a power failure.

cards.title: Spring return or double solenoid: what happens at power loss
cards.body:
- **Single solenoid, spring return** (monostable): the coil holds it over; with the coil off (or power lost) the **spring** puts it back. The cylinder goes to its rest position.
- **Double solenoid** (bistable): a pulse on one coil sends it one way, a pulse on the other sends it back. With both off it **stays** where it was: a memory.

So on a power cut, a spring-return valve moves the cylinder; a double-solenoid valve leaves it where it was. Which is safe depends on the machine: decide on purpose.
cards.more:
A spring-return valve is like a door on a closer: let go and it shuts. A double-solenoid valve is like a door with no closer: it stays wherever it was last pushed.

On a clamp that must not let go of a part when the power fails, a double-solenoid (or a spring-return valve arranged so its rest state is 'clamped') keeps the grip. On a guard door or a press, the safe state on power loss is usually 'move away' or 'stop', so the design chooses the valve and its rest state to suit, as part of the risk assessment.

In the PLC: a spring-return valve needs its output held on; a double-solenoid valve needs a short pulse on each coil, and both coils must never be on together.

cards.q: A cylinder is extended, held by a double-solenoid 5/2 valve whose 'extend' coil was pulsed. The power fails. What does the cylinder do?
options: Stays extended, if the air stays on
Retracts under its spring
Goes limp, free to move by hand
Moves to mid-stroke and stops
cards.why: A double-solenoid valve stays in its last position with both coils off, so air keeps feeding the extend side. A single-solenoid, spring-return valve would have moved.

cards.title: Speed control: meter-out
cards.body:
A cylinder's speed is set with **flow control valves**: a needle that throttles the flow, with a non-return valve that lets air through freely the other way.

On double-acting cylinders, throttle the air **leaving** the cylinder: **meter-out**. The piston then moves against a cushion of trapped air on its outgoing side, which keeps the speed steady even when the load changes.

Throttling the air going **in** (meter-in) gives a jerky, stick-slip motion, and is used mainly on single-acting cylinders.
cards.more:
Think of lowering a heavy box down a ramp on a rope: holding it back from behind (meter-out) is smooth; pushing it from the top and hoping (meter-in) lurches.

Meter-out works because the outgoing side's air is held at a pressure that pushes back on the piston; the piston can only go as fast as that air is let out.

Flow controls are usually fitted right at the cylinder ports, with the arrow on the body showing the free-flow direction. Fit one backwards and it throttles the wrong way.

cards.q: A double-acting cylinder lurches along its stroke. Its flow controls throttle the air going into the cylinder. What should change?
options: Turn them round to throttle the exhaust air (meter-out)
Raise the supply pressure to 10 bar
Fit a bigger valve with more flow
Take the flow controls off altogether
cards.why: Meter-in lets the piston stick and slip. Meter-out holds the piston against a cushion of exhaust air, so it moves steadily.

cards.q: A {bore} mm bore cylinder with a {rod} mm rod runs at {bar} bar. What force does it pull with (retracting), ignoring friction?
cards.why: Retracting, the air pushes on the ring between the rod and the bore: the bore's area less the rod's.

cards.q: A cylinder must push {kn} N at {bar} bar. What is the smallest bore that will do it in theory?
cards.why: Area needed = force ÷ pressure; then the diameter for that area. Then choose the next standard bore up, with margin for friction and speed (load at most about 70% of the theoretical force).
cards.hint: Turn F = pA round for A, then $A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4}$ round for D.

cards.q: A machine's air is isolated and the gauge at the FRL reads 0 bar. Why might a cylinder still move when you loosen a fitting?
options: Air can be trapped in it by a closed-centre valve or check valve
Cylinders store air in their spring
The gauge always reads 0 when isolated
It cannot: 0 bar at the FRL means all is safe
cards.why: The gauge shows the line, not every pocket of air downstream. Closed-centre valves, pilot-operated check valves and some soft-start valves trap air in a cylinder. Vent it deliberately (or block the load) before work.

cards.q: Checking a 40 mm bore cylinder at 6 bar. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So it can lift about 750 kg
cards.why: Bar must be turned into N/mm² (× 0.1) before multiplying by an area in mm². Sanity check: a 40 mm cylinder on shop air pushes a few hundred newtons, about the weight of one person, not 750 kg.

cards.q: A valve symbol has two squares, a solenoid on one end and a zigzag on the other. What is it?
options: A two-position valve, solenoid operated, spring return
A three-position valve with two solenoids
A flow control with a non-return valve
A pressure regulator with a gauge
cards.why: Two squares, two positions. The box with the slash is a solenoid; the zigzag is the return spring.

cards.q: Why would you choose hydraulics over pneumatics for a press that needs 200 kN?
options: Much higher pressures give big forces from a compact cylinder
Hydraulic oil is cleaner to work with than air
Hydraulics is always faster than pneumatics
Pneumatics cannot be controlled by a PLC
cards.why: Hydraulics runs at 100–250 bar or more against pneumatics' 6 or so: around 30 times the force from the same bore, and oil does not compress, so it holds position. Air suits light, fast, clean jobs.

cards.q: A single-acting, spring-return cylinder is driven by a 3/2 valve. The air fails. What does the cylinder do?
options: Returns under its spring
Stays exactly where it was
Extends under its spring
Floats freely in both directions
cards.why: With no air, the spring takes the piston back to its rest end (usually retracted). A double-acting cylinder has no spring and would stay roughly where it was.

cards.q: A regulator gauge reads {bar} bar. What is that in N/mm²?
What does 3/2 mean on a valve?
options: 3 ports and 2 positions
3 bar and 2 solenoids
3 mm bore and 2 positions
3 seconds on, 2 seconds off
cards.why: Ports/positions: supply, outlet and exhaust, in two positions. It drives a single-acting cylinder.

cards.q: A {bore} mm bore cylinder at 6 bar. Push force?
cards.why: F = pA, with 6 bar = 0.6 N/mm² and the bore's area.

cards.q: Match each port number with its job.
